# SACD Ripper network protocol (PS3 server)

`sacd_extract -i 192.0.2.10:2002` reads a disc from a PS3 running the SACD Ripper
homebrew. This document describes what goes over the wire, as implemented in
sacd-ripper's `libs/libsacd/sacd_ripper.proto`, `libs/libsacd/sacd_input.c` (client)
and `src/server.c` (PS3 server), and as reproduced by `pysacd.remote`.

The PS3 reads the disc in its Blu-ray drive and decrypts the audio areas itself.
Only plain 2048-byte logical sectors cross the network, so a server that serves an
already-decrypted ISO is indistinguishable from a PS3 to the client.

## Reading from a PS3

Both CLIs accept a PS3 address wherever they take an ISO:

```
pysacd-extract -I -i 192.0.2.10:2002          # copy the disc to an ISO
pysacd-extract -s -I -i 192.0.2.10:2002       # ISO + DSF; the disc crosses the network once
pysacd-extract -2 -s -i 192.0.2.10:2002       # DSF; only the TOCs and the stereo area are fetched
pysacd convert 192.0.2.10:2002                # tagged DSF, as for an ISO
pysacd toc --json 192.0.2.10:2002             # the TOC, without copying anything else
```

- **With `-I`,** the whole disc is streamed into the output ISO first, and any
  other outputs are produced from that file.
- **Without `-I`,** pysacd fetches only the TOCs and the areas it needs into a
  temporary sparse ISO next to the output, converts it as usual, then deletes it.
  The audio of areas you didn't ask for is skipped.
- **Dropped connections:** the connection is reopened (up to 3 times in a row,
  with backoff) and the copy resumes where it stopped, after checking that the
  disc is still the same one.

**Security:** the protocol has no authentication or encryption, so use it on trusted
networks only. pysacd treats everything a server sends as hostile: lengths, disc size,
TOC and time are all bounded, and output stays inside the output directory. See
[security](security.md#ps3-network-protocol).

## Transport

- TCP, port 2002. The PS3 listens with a backlog of 1 and serves one client at a time.
- Messages are protobuf (proto2, nanopb) with **no length prefix**. Each message is
  followed by a single `0x00` byte: nanopb stops decoding at a zero tag, so the zero
  byte marks the end of the message. Both directions use this framing.
- The client decodes responses incrementally, receiving more bytes until a complete
  message parses.
- `pysacd.remote` treats network data as untrusted. A length-delimited field larger than
  one 512-sector read plus 1 KiB, or a message with more than 16 fields, is rejected
  before anything is allocated.

## Messages

```proto
message ServerRequest {
  enum Type { DISC_OPEN = 1; DISC_CLOSE = 2; DISC_READ = 3; DISC_SIZE = 4; }
  required Type   type          = 1;
  required uint32 sector_offset = 2 [default = 0];
  required uint32 sector_count  = 3 [default = 0];
}

message ServerResponse {
  enum Type { DISC_OPENED = 1; DISC_CLOSED = 2; DISC_READ = 3; DISC_SIZE = 4; }
  required Type  type   = 1;
  required int64 result = 2;           // negative values are 10-byte varints
  optional bytes data   = 3;           // at most 512 * 2048 bytes
}
```

| request | response `result` | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `DISC_OPEN` | 0 on success | opens `/dev_bdvd`, reads the TOC and authenticates the disc; -1 if there is no disc |
| `DISC_SIZE` | total sectors | -1 if no disc is open |
| `DISC_READ` | sectors returned | `data` holds `result * 2048` bytes; see below |
| `DISC_CLOSE` | 0 | the server then closes the connection |

## Reads

A `DISC_READ` returns **at most 512 sectors** (`MAX_PROCESSING_BLOCK_SIZE`) and may return
fewer than requested. The server decrypts each audio area separately, so it cuts reads
at the area boundaries. With `[s1, e1]` the first area's audio LSN range (`track_start`,
`track_end`, inclusive) and `[s2, e2]` the second's:

| request offset | block size |
|---|---|
| `< s1` | `min(s1 - offset, 512)` |
| `s1 .. e1` | `min(e1 + 1 - offset, 512)` |
| `e1 < offset < s2` | `min(s2 - offset, 512)` |
| `s2 .. e2` | `min(e2 + 1 - offset, 512)` |

then `min(count, block size)`. On a single-area disc `s2 = e2 = 0`, so
none of the rows match after the first area and the server reuses the block size from the
previous request. Clients must loop until they have all the sectors they asked for.

The block size starts at 0 on each connection. So on a single-area disc, a new connection
whose first read starts after the audio area gets `result = 0`, and keeps getting it. That
matters when resuming after a dropped connection. `RemoteDisc` reads one sector at LSN 0
right after `DISC_OPEN`, which sets the block size before any other read. A client that
starts by reading the TOC (as `sacd_extract` does) gets the same effect.

The first time an encrypted range is read, the server checks whether the disc is
encrypted at all (some DSD 3-in-14/16 discs aren't) by looking at bytes 16-23 of the
first block. That only affects the PS3's own decryption, not the bytes sent.

## Testing without a PS3

```
pysacd ps3sim disc.iso                       # listen on 0.0.0.0:2002
sacd_extract -I -i 127.0.0.1:2002            # copy the disc back as an ISO
```

`pysacd.remote.PS3Simulator` follows `src/server.c`, including the boundary cuts and the
carried-over block size. Unlike the PS3, it listens on `127.0.0.1` unless `--host` says
otherwise, and it closes connections idle for `--idle-timeout` seconds (default 60). It also
adds knobs for testing clients: `--rate` (MB/s, to emulate
the PS3 drive), `--latency` (ms per request), `--drop-after N` (close the connection
after N reads), `--fail-lsn L` (reads covering LSN L return -1) and `--no-disc`.
From Python there are also `over_return` (send more sectors than requested) and
`disc_size` (report a different DISC_SIZE). The client must reject both. See
[docs/security.md](security.md) for the client's limits.

Checked against sacd-ripper's `sacd_extract` (built from source, 2026-10-28):

- `sacd_extract -P` prints the same disc information as with the local ISO.
- `sacd_extract -I` through the simulator produced an ISO byte-identical to the source
  (a 3.39 GB plain-DSD disc).
- `sacd_extract -2 -m -s` on a DST stereo + 5.1 disc produced 28 DSF files identical to
  a local extraction of the same ISO.

What the simulator can't reproduce: the PS3 drive's real speed and error behaviour, and
its guess about whether a disc is encrypted. A final check against a real PS3 is still
worthwhile.

## Client

- `pysacd.remote.RemoteDisc(host, port)` opens the disc and behaves as a seekable
  read-only file of 2048-byte sectors. `SACDImage`, `read_toc()` and anything else that
  takes a binary file object work unchanged. It primes the block size, as described
  under [Reads](#reads), by reading the master TOC (LSN 510–519, before the first area),
  which `fetch()` then compares on every reconnect.
- `PS3Client` is the lower-level request/response API. `read()` loops over short reads;
  `read_some()` is a single `DISC_READ`.
- `fetch(host, port, path, ranges)` copies the disc, or just the given LSN ranges, into a
  plain 2048-byte ISO.
  - Each reply is written to disk as soon as it arrives.
  - A dropped connection is reopened and the copy resumes (`retries`, `backoff`).
  - Sectors outside `ranges` stay holes in a sparse file.
- `needed_ranges(disc, total, areas)` gives the ranges needed to convert `areas`:
  everything except the audio of the other areas.
- `fetch_temp()` combines the two for the CLIs: it fetches the needed ranges into a
  temporary sparse ISO, which the native engine then reads like any other image.

`pysacd-extract -i HOST:PORT` and `pysacd convert HOST:PORT` use these. Checked
through the simulator on a 3.39 GB plain-DSD disc:

- `pysacd-extract -I` produced a byte-identical ISO.
- `pysacd-extract -s` and `pysacd convert` produced the same DSF files as from the
  local ISO (24 tracks), and removed their temporary files.
